take.head: Browns edge the Steelers in a field-goal game
take.lean:
Deshaun Watson throws into a Steelers secondary without Joey Porter Jr., and Jalen Ramsey (wrist) and Brandin Echols (concussion) are both questionable. Watson has been an above-average passer through three weeks. Aaron Rodgers has been one of the worst passers in the league. That gap matters more than any name on the field.

Cleveland's problem is up front. Elgton Jenkins and Teven Jenkins are both out, so two rookies start on the line against a Pittsburgh rush that sacks the quarterback on 8.6 percent of pass plays. Watson will take hits and some drives will die. He has an answer, though: he took 36.7 percent of Cleveland's carries last week and has beaten his projection three weeks running. His running holds up even against a defense that allows the fifth-fewest points to quarterbacks.

He has to keep the ball, because the Browns' running backs are no help. Cleveland's run game is the league's worst. Quinshon Judkins gets most of the carries and has still fallen short of his projection every week. He was limited at practice for personal reasons, and Raheim Sanders takes passing-down snaps. Pittsburgh ranks 22nd against backs, which keeps Judkins from a disaster, but not much more.

So the passing game carries Cleveland. Denzel Boston plays nearly every snap, and with Porter out he draws the easier corners. Harold Fannin Jr. drew 30 percent of the targets last week, but Pittsburgh ranks 8th against tight ends, so he lands near his number rather than repeating that game.

Pittsburgh is priced like last year's offense, which scored 23.4 a game with Rodgers playing well. This year's version swings from a 4.0-point week to a 22.7-point week, and the 22.7 came against Cincinnati. Jaylen Warren is the engine with Rico Dowdle out. He got 73.9 percent of the carries last week, but Cleveland's defense ranks 9th against backs, so the volume pays without a breakout.

The Steelers' path is outside. Cleveland's defense ranks 26th against wide receivers, and DK Metcalf is the receiver Rodgers looks for when a drive needs a play. That gets Pittsburgh into the red zone. Finishing is the problem: the Steelers score touchdowns on a third of their trips, and the Browns do little better at 37.5 percent. Both offenses stall inside the 20 and trade field goals, and the home team with the better quarterback this season wins the last exchange.
take.vs: Disagree on the side: the market expects PIT 20.5, CLE 18. Rodgers' passing doesn't back that up, and Cleveland's home field and better quarterback win a game this tight.
take.risk: PIT's rush overwhelms CLE's two rookie linemen, Watson takes sacks and turns it over, and Warren's workload breaks a long run.

ats.edge: PIT is priced on last year's 23.4-point offense; Rodgers has been among the league's worst passers this year, Watson above average

take.head: Colts edge it, Mariota keeps Washington close
take.lean:
Jonathan Taylor runs into a wall in London. Washington's defense ranks 2nd against running backs and has stuffed the run all season. That puts this game on Daniel Jones's arm, and Washington's pass defense is where the points are. It ranks dead last against wide receivers and 31st against tight ends.

Jones has been the worst part of the Colts' offense. He has been sacked often, his passes have gained almost nothing, and he keeps giving the ball away. Some of that is bad luck: the Colts lost 3 of 4 fumbles. He was efficient all of last year, and this is the defense where he gets back on track. Keenan Allen is out and Alec Pierce is on IR, so his throws have only two places to go. Josh Downs drew a 31.4 percent target share last week. Tyler Warren's share has gone up every week, and he plays almost every snap. Expect both to beat their projections while Taylor gets his carries and few yards.

The Colts won't pull away, though, because their own defense is just as bad. Indianapolis ranks 29th against quarterbacks and gives up more than 30 points a game. Marcus Mariota has kept Washington's passing game working without Jayden Daniels. He scored 20.4 points last week, many of them on his own runs, and those runs don't depend on who is catching passes. With Terry McLaurin and Rachaad White out, Stefon Diggs gets nearly every short throw that matters.

Washington's ground game is the weak spot. Indianapolis ranks 28th against backs, but Jacory Croskey-Merritt has done little with a lead role. Austin Ekeler now takes part of that work, which keeps both of them near their projections. Washington's points come from Mariota and Diggs moving the ball through the air.

This turns into a passing game on both sides, with two secondaries that can't stop anyone. Indianapolis wins because Jones has the better targets left. Washington stays within a field goal because the Colts' turnovers give it extra possessions.
take.vs: Higher on both teams. The implied 21 for Washington ignores an Indianapolis defense ranked 29th against QBs, and two leaky pass defenses push the total over.
take.risk: Taylor breaks through Washington's run defense and the Colts pull away on the ground, or Jones throws away more possessions.

ats.edge: The move to IND by 4.5 over-prices Daniels' absence; Mariota has kept the pass game working and Jones keeps giving the ball away.

take.head: Cardinals edge it; Giants cover at home
take.lean:
Jacoby Brissett gets all day against a Giants pass rush that has almost nothing left. New York sacked the quarterback on just 1.0 percent of pass plays this season, and that was with Brian Burns. Burns is now out for the season with a torn ACL, so Brissett gets a clean pocket and an easy afternoon of reading the field.

Brissett gets the ball to Trey McBride and Michael Wilson. Wilson drew 34.0 percent of the targets last week. A Giants defense that ranks 28th against the pass has no answer for him on the outside. McBride works the middle on volume, the way he has all season. With James Conner on IR, Jeremiyah Love handled 77.8 percent of the carries last week and gets the early-down work against a Giants run defense that is ordinary.

Arizona's offense has one weakness, and it keeps this game close. The Cardinals almost never hit a big play. Their drives are long strings of short completions, and long drives stall. Arizona moves the ball between the 20s all day but settles for field goals too often to pull away.

The Giants want to run, and they hit the wrong defense for it. New York passes only 38.2 percent of the time when the game is close. Arizona's run defense is one of the league's stingiest. Cam Skattebo needed 20 carries to reach 60 yards against the Titans, and this front is tougher. Expect a lot of short runs.

That puts the game in Jameis Winston's hands, which sounds like bad news. He has been dreadful through 55 pass plays this season. But Arizona's pass defense ranks 30th and lost Will Johnson, a defensive back who played 89.5 percent of snaps before going on IR. Winston will throw into tight windows no matter who lines up across from him. Against this secondary, enough of those throws get completed. Malik Nabers took 28.6 percent of the targets last week and gets the soft coverage. Isaiah Likely faces a defense that ranks 28th against tight ends.

The market swung this game completely when Jaxson Dart went on IR, and that swing went far enough. Arizona's quarterback is better and should win, but a Cardinals team without big plays doesn't build a lead the Giants can't erase late. Arizona wins a game that's still in doubt in the fourth quarter. Brissett and Wilson are the best starts in it, and Nabers is the Giants player to trust.
take.vs: Agree Arizona wins, but by less. The Giants land near their 21 because Arizona's secondary leaks, and Arizona's lack of big plays keeps it short of 23.5.
take.risk: Winston keeps throwing it to the other team the way he has in 2026, and Brissett's clean pocket turns this into a two-score Arizona win.

ats.edge: Arizona's 30th-ranked pass defense, without Will Johnson, lets Winston and Nabers keep the Giants within a field goal.

take.head: Stroud, Lamb feast; Dallas keeps it close
take.lean:
Stroud gets Nico Collins back against a Dallas secondary that ranks 31st in the league at stopping the pass. That secondary gets almost no help up front: Dallas sacks the quarterback on just 2.1 percent of pass plays.

Houston needs this matchup, because little else on its offense works. Its run game is among the league's worst, and David Montgomery and Woody Marks split the carries. The line gives up sacks more often than the league average. In week 3, with Collins out, Stroud scored 11.7 points and the Texans put up 17 in a loss to the Colts.

Collins changes that. In week 1 he drew a 27.0 percent target share, and Stroud finally has a receiver the defense has to account for on every snap. Houston throws early and often instead of running Montgomery into the line. Dalton Schultz goes back to a secondary role after picking up extra targets while Collins was out.

Dallas answers the same way. Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb have been nearly perfect together, and Houston is missing linebackers Azeez Al-Shaair and Henry To'oTo'o, the two players who cover the middle of the field. The Texans already give up the 30th-most points to receivers. Without those linebackers, Lamb and Jake Ferguson find open space on routes across the middle.

Houston wins one matchup clearly: its pass rush sacks quarterbacks on 10.1 percent of pass plays. Dallas's line rarely gives up sacks, though, and Prescott gets the ball out on time. The rush gets home a few times without stopping the drives.

Javonte Williams takes the hit on the Dallas side. Houston gives up the fewest points to running backs in the league, and Dallas's own run game is below average. With an easy matchup through the air, the Cowboys put the game on Prescott, and Williams gets his touches without the big runs.

Expect a back-and-forth game through the air. Houston has the home crowd and gets back the receiver it has missed, so it edges the game late. Still, Dallas's passing game is the best unit on the field and keeps the game within a field goal. George Pickens gets his share of the targets behind Lamb, but he does not have a big game.
take.vs: Close to the market on Houston, but Dallas scores more than its implied 22.8: Houston's missing linebackers and a defense 30th against receivers let Prescott keep pace.
take.risk: Houston's pass rush sacks Prescott and stalls drives, or Houston's line gives up sacks again and Stroud never gets time to find Collins.

ats.edge: Houston plays without its top two linebackers and gives up the 30th-most WR points; Dak and Lamb keep this within a field goal.

take.head: Packers edge it, Bucs cover behind Irving
take.lean:
Jalon Daniels is an undrafted rookie making his first start, and he gets a Green Bay defense that has given up 30.3 points a game. The debut is softer than the quarterback change suggests. Baker Mayfield's passing was already among the league's worst before he hurt his thumb, so Tampa isn't losing a passing game that worked. It is swapping one that stalled for one with a quarterback who can run.

Daniels' running matters most against Tampa's biggest flaw. Bucs passers have been sacked on 10.7% of pass plays, and a quarterback who runs turns some of those sacks into scrambles. His running also opens room for Bucky Irving. Green Bay allows the most fantasy points to running backs in the league, and Irving's carry share climbed to 71.4 last week. His sore glute let him practice Thursday, and he is the Bucs player to start with confidence. Kenny Gainwell stays an afterthought.

The Bucs' passing game shrinks to short throws. Emeka Egbuka leads Tampa's receivers in targets and Cade Otton plays nearly every snap, so they are the rookie's first reads. Chris Godwin Jr. missed Wednesday's practice with a sore ankle and drops to third in line.

Green Bay's offense has the opposite problem. The Packers run for 48.7 yards a game, Josh Jacobs is on the commissioner's exempt list, and the offensive line is missing starters, Jacob Monk among them. Tampa's run defense is among the league's best. MarShawn Lloyd has nowhere to go, and this becomes Jordan Love's game whether Green Bay wants it or not.

Love has the receivers to carry it. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden have both drawn heavy targets, and Tampa is without defensive back Benjamin Morrison and pass rusher Rueben Bain. Tampa still holds receivers down overall, so Love lands near his projection, not past it. Tucker Kraft finds the open space, against a defense that ranks 21st against tight ends.

That leaves a close game settled by Love's arm late. Tampa's fumbles keep the Packers in front: the Bucs have lost 4 of their 5. But with both defenses giving up points this easily, the scoring runs past what the market expects, and Tampa stays within a field goal.
take.vs: Agree on Green Bay winning, but Tampa scores more. The total fell after Mayfield's injury, yet his passing was already poor and Green Bay's defense allows 30.3 points a game.
take.risk: Daniels melts under the rush Tampa already allows, the fumbles keep coming, and Love's receivers beat a thin secondary for a two-score Packers win.

ats.edge: Mayfield was already passing at a bottom-tier level; the line moved to GB as if losing him were a big downgrade.

take.head: Lawrence beats a thin Bengals secondary
take.lean:
Trevor Lawrence comes to Cincinnati playing the best football of his career, and he faces a Bengals secondary that is missing pieces. Kyle Dugger is out, Bryan Cook is questionable with an ankle and Jalen Davis is on IR. That leaves the back end short on bodies against a passer who is getting far more out of each throw than he did in 2025.

Cincinnati's defense looks better on paper this year. It ranks 8th against the pass, but it built that rank with its safeties healthy, and the same unit gave up 28.9 points a game last season. Quarterbacks already score well against it: it ranks 22nd in points allowed to the position. With the depth thin behind the cornerbacks, Lawrence gets clean throws over the middle.

Jacksonville doesn't settle for field goals. The Jaguars have turned 88.9% of their red-zone trips into touchdowns, so their drives end in the end zone. Bhayshul Tuten benefits most. He handles half the carries and has beaten his projection every week. Parker Washington leads the targets and keeps getting open against the backup safeties. Brenton Strange has gone quiet, but Cincinnati gives tight ends the 24th-most points, so this is his week to turn targets into catches.

The Bengals have the harder job. Jacksonville's defense allows 12.0 points a game, and quarterbacks score less against it than against all but two teams. Joe Burrow keeps the passing game moving, but in this matchup his production runs through one man. Ja'Marr Chase drew 32.4% of the targets last week and gets that volume again. The Bengals have nobody else they can count on.

The running game won't take any pressure off Burrow. Cincinnati's runs lose ground on most plays, and Jacksonville ranks 6th against backs. Chase Brown has fallen short of his projection two weeks running, and that continues. Mike Gesicki goes up against a defense that ranks 7th against tight ends.

The game comes down to touchdowns against field goals. The Bengals have scored touchdowns on only half of their red-zone trips. Jacksonville's defense has allowed touchdowns on 20.0% of opponents' trips. The Jaguars score touchdowns on their drives and Cincinnati settles for field goals on too many of theirs. That gap holds all afternoon, and Jacksonville leaves with the win.

take.risk: Burrow and Chase hit big plays on a JAX defense that allows WRs 25.9 a game, and Cincinnati scores touchdowns instead of field goals.

take.head: Rams cover as Eagles run out of receivers
take.lean:
Stafford will have time to throw against an Eagles defense that hasn't taken the ball away once in 3 games. Philadelphia sacks the quarterback on 3.1% of pass plays, about half the league rate. Now it also plays without Baun, the linebacker who was on the field for nearly every snap. That leaves a soft middle and a pass rush that doesn't get home, which suits a Rams offense that passes more than most when the game is close.

The Rams win this game on throws. Philadelphia's pass defense ranks 23rd, and its defense ranks 25th against receivers. Adams has carried the passing game with 15 catches for 332 yards the last two weeks. Nacua returns from 2 missed games, and the Rams will ease him back. That keeps Adams as the first read for another week, and he beats his projection. Stafford threw for 390 yards last week. Against this rush he moves the ball all afternoon.

Los Angeles stalls near the goal line. The Rams have scored touchdowns on just 45.5% of their red-zone trips, and those stalled drives turn into field goals. That keeps the game close enough to stay interesting. Kyren Williams is the goal-line back after taking 65.2% of the carries last week. Philadelphia ranks 10th against backs, so he lands near his number and doesn't blow past it.

Philadelphia can't match the Rams through the air. Its passing game was below average even with Smith and Goedert, and the offense scored 18.3 points a game. Both are out. That leaves Wicks, Lemon and the recently signed Moore at receiver, with Ertz at tight end, against a pass defense that ranks 7th. The Rams' rush is thin too, with Garrett on injured reserve and Donald out. Hurts gets time, but he has nobody to throw to. His runs keep him a usable starter, but he doesn't get above a mid-range finish.

Wicks is the one Eagles pass catcher to start. He has drawn 20% of the targets with Smith in the lineup. Without Smith he's the first read on every pass play, and against the Rams' 13th-ranked defense against receivers he clears a low projection. Barkley goes the other way. The Rams rank 7th against backs, and a Philadelphia team that trails all game hands him fewer carries than his 10.8 projection needs.

On the Rams' side, Higbee has the worst draw: Philadelphia ranks 2nd against tight ends. Ertz has a similar problem across the field against a Rams defense that ranks 5th against the position. The Rams build a lead with Stafford's arm and keep it with field goals. Philadelphia's offense doesn't have the pieces to get back into it.

take.head: Bills cover, Patriots stall in the red zone
take.lean:
Drake Maye drops back behind a patched-up line. Greg Van Roten is on IR, Mike Onwenu is hurt and Morgan Moses is questionable. Buffalo's front reaches the quarterback more often than most, and Maye has no A.J. Brown to throw to quickly with Brown on IR. Maye scored 3.8 last week, and this line gives him no more time than the one that produced that.

The pressure feeds New England's real problem: it can't finish drives. The Patriots score 12 a game and have reached the end zone on just 1 of 7 red-zone trips. Maye was far better in 2025, and Buffalo has given up 26 a game, so New England moves the ball through the middle of the field. Then it stalls close to the goal line and kicks field goals.

Buffalo's offense has a tougher test than its scoring suggests. New England's defense ranks 4th against the pass and allows the fewest points to tight ends. That is bad news for Dalton Kincaid. But Christian Gonzalez is out, and that changes where Josh Allen throws. DJ Moore drew 38.5 percent of the targets last week, and now he works the outside against the Patriots' backup corners.

Christian Barmore is out too, which opens the middle for James Cook. He took 72.7 percent of the carries last week, and a Buffalo lead keeps feeding him. Allen lands close to his projection. The Patriots allow the fifth-fewest points to quarterbacks, and Cook handles the short scores Allen usually runs in himself.

Once Buffalo leads by more than a score, New England has to throw, and Mack Hollins gets the volume. He drew 30.0 percent of the targets last week. Buffalo ranks 29th against receivers, and its corner Christian Benford is questionable. The Patriots' backfield goes the other way. Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson split the carries, and falling behind takes the run game away from both.

Buffalo wins clearly, but not in a shootout. New England's pass defense holds the Bills below their usual scoring, and the Patriots' red-zone failures cap their side. That keeps the combined score well short of what the market expects.

take.head: Jets stay inside the hook at Soldier Field
take.lean:
Tyson Bagent takes over a Bears offense that was rolling, and he faces the one thing the Jets do well: stop the run. New York's run defense ranks among the league's best this season, so a backup quarterback won't get the easy early downs he needs. Bagent's 9 pass plays this year went badly. Case Keenum ran this offense well in last week's 27-7 win over the Eagles, but Bagent gets the start, and left tackle Braxton Jones is out in front of him.

That puts D'Andre Swift in a tough spot. He has scored about 10 points in each of the last two weeks while getting more than half the carries, and the Jets' front won't give him more room than that. His floor comes from catching passes, and Bagent will check down to him often. Kyle Monangai's share of the work keeps shrinking, and running into this defense won't turn that around.

So Chicago has to throw, and Luther Burden III is the target. His target share has gone up every week, to 32.4 percent against Philadelphia, and the Jets' pass defense sits 17th, right in the middle of the league. Mayfield was throwing worse, play for play, than Daniels has, and the Bucs scored 19 points a game with him. Daniels' real danger is his line. It has allowed 16 sacks, and Tampa Bay has 9 giveaways in four games. Dallas, though, barely gets to the passer, with sacks on only 3.1 percent of pass plays. Dak Prescott still runs one of the league's best passing games, and the Dallas offense works through CeeDee Lamb, who caught 17 of 21 targets against Houston. Lamb lands near his projection by catching a lot of short passes, not by breaking long ones. George Pickens is the receiver who gets squeezed out. Jake Ferguson is the opening: Tampa Bay ranks 26th against tight ends, and the middle of the field is where Prescott goes when the outside is covered.

Javonte Williams' three-touchdown game against Houston doesn't carry over. Tampa Bay ranks 6th against backs and stuffs runs better than almost anyone, so Dallas moves the ball through the air and finishes some drives with field goals instead of short touchdown runs.

The game follows that pattern. Dallas leads all night, but its defense gives up big plays on 11.2 percent of snaps, and Daniels connects on enough of them to keep the Bucs within one score late. Every carry Daniels keeps is one Bucky Irving doesn't get, and Irving's role keeps shrinking with a running quarterback in the backfield.

When Love can't hand off, he throws quick to Lloyd as a check-down and keeps the passing game short. That kind of passing does not beat this secondary. take.head: Texans win, but Titans stay inside a TD

So the ball goes to Nico Collins. Tank Dell is out, and Collins drew 30.8 percent of the targets in his first game back. Nobody else on this roster demands the ball. The weak spot is Stroud's protection. Right tackle Braden Smith is out, and left tackle Aireontae Ersery missed Thursday and Friday practice with an illness. Tony Pollard owns the backfield now that Tyjae Spears has faded. Houston gives up the ninth-fewest points to backs, though, so Pollard gets volume without a big day.

Houston controls the game through Collins and builds a lead. Tennessee keeps answering through the air against a defense still learning its new play-caller, and the Titans' late drives against soft coverage bring the game back inside the number.

take.head: Taylor and the rain carry the Colts past PIT

Jonathan Taylor runs into a Steelers defense that ranks 24th against backs, and he does it in a downpour, with a 94 percent chance of rain. Indianapolis runs the ball as well as almost anyone this season and throws it as badly as anyone. Wet weather takes away the part of their offense that doesn't work and leaves them the part that does.

Daniel Jones is the reason the Colts can't throw. He has scored 7.9 points in each of the last two weeks, threw for 143 yards in London, and keeps turning the ball over. In the rain, Indianapolis has no reason to ask him to do much. The plan is Taylor on early downs, Taylor near the goal line and Taylor to finish. That plan already works: the Colts score touchdowns on 75 percent of their red-zone trips. Jones falls short of his projection again. Taylor carries the fantasy value for this side.

Pittsburgh's secondary is thin, with Jamel Dean out and Jalen Ramsey playing through a wrist injury. On a dry day that is how the Colts' receivers would hurt them. On this day Jones can't take advantage. Josh Downs lives on Jones's accuracy and gets nothing in the rain. Tyler Warren's short catches survive the weather, and that keeps him near his number.

The Steelers need Aaron Rodgers, and his season says that's a problem. Their passing game ranks near the bottom of the league, and he gets sacked on 7.6 percent of his pass plays. Indianapolis's defense is soft against quarterbacks, 28th in the league, with only 2 takeaways, so Rodgers will move the ball some. He threw for 299 yards and three touchdowns last week, but he also threw two interceptions. A slick ball makes deep throws harder for DK Metcalf, though his target share keeps him close to his line. That leaves Jaylen Warren as Pittsburgh's best fantasy play. He had nearly every carry last week, and the Colts rank 23rd against backs. Rico Dowdle practiced Friday, though, and his return takes some of that work, so Warren lands near his projection rather than over it.

In a slow, wet, low-scoring game, three points is a lot of cushion, and the team with the run game that works has it. Indianapolis gets ahead and closes it out with Taylor's carries late.

take.head: Raiders keep it close as Bowers feasts
take.lean:
Kirk Cousins walks into Foxborough against a Patriots secondary missing four cornerbacks, and the two that matter are Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis. When they were healthy, New England's pass defense ranked 5th and held tight ends to 4.3 points a game, the fewest in the league. Without them, that ranking describes players who are not in uniform Sunday.

Brock Bowers is the first to cash in. He came back from his knee injury and took 43.3 percent of the targets in his first game, and he practiced in full this week. With the corners gone, New England's safeties and linebackers have to cover him with no help outside. Cousins has scored over 20 points in each of his last three games, and his line keeps him clean: he has been sacked on just 3.4 percent of pass plays. Jalen Nailor is out with a concussion, so Tre Tucker plays more of the snaps outside, and the backups he faces are a big step down.

What keeps Las Vegas from winning outright is that it can't run. Ashton Jeanty is active, but his ankle and foot cost him practice time, and he runs behind one of the league's worst run games. His snaps were already falling before the injury, and Mike Washington Jr. is taking more of the carries. Expect the Raiders to drive the field through the air and stall in the red zone.

On the other side, Drake Maye faces a Raiders pass rush that gets home, with sacks on 8.2 percent of pass plays, behind a pass defense that ranks 3rd. This is not the Maye of 2025. New England has given the ball away 10 times in four games, and its offense scores 16.2 points a game. Much of that is fumbles, and fumbles don't keep happening at that rate. That bounce-back, plus home field, is why New England still wins. Maye's legs keep his fantasy day steady even when the throws don't come.

Hunter Henry gets the matchup to use. Las Vegas has allowed 15.1 points a game to tight ends, 28th in the league, and Henry works the middle of the field where that pass rush can't reach him. Romeo Doubs gets the worst of it: the Raiders rank 7th against receivers, and two touchdowns made last week's line look better than his volume.

New England's run game is no better than the Raiders'. Rhamondre Stevenson is active through his knee injury, and his share of the carries keeps rising, but neither backfield will control this game. It stays within one score until the end, and a Raiders team that throws at will against backup corners stays inside the number.

Minnesota's own offense won't win this through the air. Kyler Murray gets sacked on 9.9% of pass plays. Left tackle Christian Darrisaw is out and guard Donovan Jackson is done for the year. Justin Jefferson is questionable with the ankle injury that knocked him out after 12% of the snaps in Week 3. He plans to play, but a hobbled Jefferson behind this line is a decoy, not a WR1. T.J. Hockenson is still the read Murray trusts: he caught all 13 targets last week, and New Orleans ranks 26th against tight ends.

The Vikings win this on the ground. The Saints allow 32.2 points a game to running backs, the most in the league, and linebacker Kaden Elliss is out. Aaron Jones gets most of the carries and a quarter of the targets, so a weak run defense turns straight into fantasy points for him. Murray lands near his projection: the Saints are 27th against the pass, but his line keeps cutting his plays short.

New Orleans runs a lot of plays. Against this defense, more snaps means more chances to fumble. Minnesota wins it with the slow approach: Jones keeps the chains moving, Hockenson converts third downs, and the Vikings' pass rush ends drives.

take.head: Daniels wins it; Giants cover through the air
take.lean:
Jayden Daniels comes back from his elbow injury to face a Giants front that can't get to the quarterback. Brian Burns and Chauncey Golston are both on injured reserve, and New York has sacked passers on just 2.1 percent of pass plays. Daniels practiced fully all week. With time to throw and his legs on a rainy field, he is the most reliable scorer in this game.

The trouble is who he throws to. Stefon Diggs is out, and Terry McLaurin is a game-time decision with a hamstring injury. That makes Antonio Williams the top read for an offense that has struggled to make big plays. The run game won't bail him out. Washington's ground attack is among the league's worst, and Jacory Croskey-Merritt was limited all week with a groin injury. When drives stall, the ball goes to Rachaad White, the passing-down back.

That keeps the Giants in the game, because Washington's defense has the most holes of anyone on the field. It allows 30.5 points a game and is missing three safeties: Nick Cross, Percy Butler and Tyler Owens. The middle of the field is open, and Washington ranks 30th against tight ends. Isaiah Likely drew 41.4 percent of the targets last week, and he is Jameis Winston's natural outlet when the rain takes away deep shots. Malik Nabers practiced fully by Friday after his knee scare, and he faces a secondary that ranks 28th against receivers.

Winston is why New York doesn't win. He has been a poor passer since Jaxson Dart went down, his line gives up sacks, and a wet ball makes his turnovers worse. Cam Skattebo won't carry the offense for him either. Washington ranks 6th against backs, and the Giants' run game is as bad as Washington's.

It plays out as a sloppy game that still clears the total, with both offenses scoring through the air against defenses that are missing key players. Daniels wins it for Washington, but Likely and Nabers keep the Giants inside the hook.
take.vs: Close to the implied 22.5-19. WAS scores a bit more with Daniels back against a rush without Burns, and NYG scores a bit more against a secondary missing three safeties.
take.risk: Winston turns it over in the rain and McLaurin plays a full game, so Washington pulls away past the hook.

take.head: Broncos win ugly behind a broken Chargers line
take.lean:
Justin Herbert drops back behind a makeshift line. Joe Alt and Trevor Penning are out and Rashawn Slater is on IR, which leaves backups at both tackle spots. Herbert was already being sacked on 8.3% of his pass plays with a healthier line, the main reason the Chargers are 0-4. Denver's pass rush is not as fierce as it was last year, but it doesn't need to be when the edges are this weak.

The Chargers do have one real opening. Denver has ruled out both starting corners, Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss. The problem is that Herbert has few receivers left to use it. Quentin Johnston is out and Ladd McConkey is not expected to play after missing every practice, so Tre Harris is the clear No. 1. He already drew more than a fifth of the targets in Week 3, and he gets more volume and softer coverage here. Oronde Gadsden II took a quarter of the targets last week. He stays involved as a short option, but with Herbert under pressure those throws won't go far.

The pressure also pushes the backfield toward Keaton Mitchell. Omarion Hampton's snaps fell from 63% to 35% over three weeks while Mitchell's grew, and Mitchell is the back who catches the quick throws when the pocket collapses. Denver gives up the 25th-most fantasy points to running backs, so Mitchell's catches add up. Hampton needs a touchdown to hit his number.

Denver's offense is ordinary, but it is clean. Bo Nix is sacked on only 3.5% of his pass plays, and the Broncos have 4 giveaways all season. The Chargers' defense is missing Derwin James and Donte Jackson, so Nix can make the safe throws to Jaylen Waddle. Waddle has been the top target, and he gets more room without James patrolling the middle.

With Jonah Coleman on IR, RJ Harvey runs Denver's backfield as a receiver. He caught all 10 of his targets last week, and the Chargers' defense ranks 22nd against backs. J.K. Dobbins still gets the early-down carries, but he hasn't reached his projection in three weeks. Courtland Sutton is fading behind Waddle and Harvey.

The Chargers have 9 giveaways in four games, and Herbert threw two interceptions and lost a fumble last week. Denver doesn't have to play well. It only has to avoid mistakes while the Chargers make theirs, and that adds up to a Denver lead late that neither offense scores enough to change.

take.risk: The Chargers' backup tackles hold up, Harris beats Denver's backup corners deep early, and a turnover-free Herbert keeps this a field-goal game.

take.head: Goff wins it, McBride keeps Arizona in it
take.lean:
Goff gets to throw at a Cardinals pass defense that ranks 31st, and that is the cleanest edge on the field. Arizona has been beaten through the air all season. Against the run it is the opposite: the Cardinals rank 8th against backs. So Detroit wins this game in the air, not on the ground.

That changes how Detroit's touches add up. Goff, St. Brown and LaPorta carry the offense, and Arizona ranks 29th against both receivers and tight ends. Gibbs still sees every carry and his share of the passes, but his carries run into the one part of Arizona's defense that holds. His points have to come from catches, and that leaves him short of a top-tier week.

The trouble for Detroit is that its own defense is worse. The Lions allow 31.8 points a game, and they give up the most fantasy points in the league to quarterbacks and to tight ends. Branch, Ya-Sin, Maddox and Harper are all out, which puts Chuck Clark and Christian Izien at safety. Detroit needs to win a shootout, and it is not built to end one early.

Arizona can't hit that weak spot with Harrison, who is inactive while the Cardinals finish trading him. That narrows Brissett's reads to McBride and Wilson, and both were already getting plenty of targets. McBride saw 12 targets last week and gained only 31 yards. This week those targets come against a Lions defense that is last against tight ends and has no healthy depth behind its starters. Wilson takes the outside work and gets Detroit's backup corners.

Arizona's ceiling is limited by how it moves the ball. The Cardinals almost never make big plays. They move in short steps, so drives are long, possessions are few and the clock keeps running. That keeps Arizona within one score late, but it also keeps the game from turning into the track meet the market expects. Brissett lands near his usual output: Detroit gives up plenty to quarterbacks, but he threw three interceptions last week.

The Cardinals' backfield stays split. Love is off the injury report, but he has been on the field for under half the snaps in two of the last three games while sharing work with Allgeier. When Arizona trails in the second half, the game goes through McBride, not the running backs.

Detroit wins because Goff has more ways to score than Brissett does. Arizona has the one matchup Detroit can't cover, and McBride gets the Cardinals into the final minutes still one score behind.

take.head: Niners win a grinder at Lumen Field
take.lean:
Brock Purdy hasn't been sacked in four games, and Sunday he faces the best defense on his schedule. Seattle allows the second-fewest fantasy points to quarterbacks and to wide receivers. Purdy's pace slows here. No quarterback keeps adding points at the rate he has through four weeks, and this is the week his numbers come down.

Coming down is not falling apart. The 49ers have turned the ball over once all season, and they finish drives: 85.7 percent of their red-zone trips end in touchdowns. Seattle's coverage on the outside pushes the ball inside to George Kittle. He has drawn at least a fifth of the targets in each of the last two weeks, and Seattle ranks only 13th against tight ends. Mike Evans is coming off a rib injury, faces the part of this defense Seattle does best, and comes up short.

Christian McCaffrey lands near his projection. Seattle's defense shuts down the run, and Kyle Juszczyk is out as his lead blocker, but McCaffrey gets enough short catches to keep his floor.

Seattle's bigger problem is its own offense. It has the league's worst run game, and Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price are both out. Emanuel Wilson has the job and most of the carries. Two touchdowns made his 25.5-point week, and those won't repeat on a run game this weak. Still, George Holani is limited with sore ribs, so Wilson keeps the volume against a 49ers defense that ranks 21st against backs and lands near his projection.

That leaves Sam Darnold, who has been about average this season, throwing mostly to one man. Jaxon Smith-Njigba has drawn 30 percent or more of the targets in each of the last three weeks. The 49ers are without Nick Bosa up front and safety Marques Sigle behind, and that is where Seattle scores. Smith-Njigba beats his projection. Darnold doesn't. He threw only 22 passes last week, and when the run game stalls, Seattle's drives stall too.

Neither offense runs many plays, and both defenses rarely give up big ones, so the game stays low-scoring. The red zone decides it. Seattle's defense has let 75 percent of opponents' trips inside the 20 end in touchdowns, and San Francisco is the offense built to cash them in. Seattle settles for field goals and the 49ers don't.

take.head: Falcons run past a Baltimore without Lamar
take.lean:
Derrick Henry runs into one of the stingiest run defenses in the league, and Lamar Jackson isn't beside him to pull a defender away. Atlanta allows the 7th-fewest points to backs. With Tyler Huntley at quarterback, the Falcons can crowd the line and dare Baltimore to throw.

Huntley will throw, but mostly short. In relief at Tennessee he went 8-of-9 for 63 yards, and Baltimore didn't score in that second half. That is a quarterback who takes what's open, not one who stretches a defense. The open throws go to Zay Flowers. He's active despite the foot injury, and he drew 34.5 percent of the targets last week. Atlanta lost A.J. Terrell, and its defense gives up the 26th-most points to receivers. Mark Andrews gets the other short throws over the middle, against a defense that ranks 22nd against tight ends. Henry gets his carries and a short touchdown chance, but not the yards his projection expects.

The game swings on the other side of the ball. Atlanta has one of the league's best run games, and Baltimore's run defense has been worse than league average this year. Trey Hendrickson is out, too. Bijan Robinson just ran for 145 yards and two scores against the Saints, and this is the same kind of matchup. Brian Robinson keeps the goal-line work behind him. Three touchdowns last week won't repeat, but he scores often enough to stay in the flex picture.

That ground game shrinks Michael Penix Jr.'s workload. Atlanta passes only 41 percent of the time when the game is close. Penix has played well in his two games, but long drives on the ground mean fewer throws and a lower ceiling. Drake London still gets his share. Baltimore ranks 25th against receivers, so he lands near his number even in a run-first plan.

Turnovers are the one way Baltimore steals this. Atlanta has eight giveaways in four games, while Baltimore has two. Hand Huntley a short field and the Ravens hang around. If the Falcons hold onto the ball, they control the clock, keep Huntley to short throws and win by more than a field goal.

take.head: Rams squeak by; Bills stay inside a field goal
take.lean:
Josh Allen faces the toughest pass defense he has seen this year, and he brings a short-handed receiver room. The Rams rank second in the league at stopping the pass and give up the fewest points to tight ends. DJ Moore is questionable with a shoulder injury.

Buffalo's answer is the one it always has: Allen's legs and a plan that leans on the run. The Rams shut down running backs too, though, so James Cook spends the night grinding for short gains. The Bills' scoring comes from Allen scrambling and pushing it in near the goal line. Buffalo has turned 73.3 percent of its red-zone trips into touchdowns. Dalton Kincaid gets nothing against this defense, so the throws go to Keon Coleman, who just turned seven targets into 116 yards and a score.

The Rams' offense is why this stays close. It averages only 21.2 points a game. Against the Eagles, Matthew Stafford threw 51 passes with no touchdowns and two interceptions. The Bills' pass defense still gives him room to bounce back. It allows more points to receivers than any defense in the league, and Ed Oliver is out of the middle of the line.

Puka Nacua is the one who cashes in. He drew 24 percent of the targets in his first game back from the hip injury and turned them into nine catches for 125 yards. With Nacua back, Davante Adams goes from top option to second option. Kyren Williams played 83 percent of the snaps last week and catches as much as he runs. Against a Buffalo defense that ranks 26th against backs, he gets plenty of both.

That gets the Rams the win, but not by much. Los Angeles has 8 giveaways in four games, and Buffalo hits quarterbacks more than most defenses. Every Stafford turnover hands a Bills offense that scores in the red zone a short field. The Rams lead most of the night, but Allen keeps getting the ball back with a chance to tie it, and the margin never gets wide.
